item.title: Chiricahua monument in Arizona is now the 64th US national park
item.description: New designation of the Land of Standing-Up Rocks, known for its historic rock spires, passed with bipartisan support An area of towering rock spires in south-eastern Arizona known among Native Americans as the Land of Standing-Up Rocks has become the nation’s newest national park. Legislation to create Chiricahua national park was sent to the White House and Donald Trump signed it on Tuesday. It passed Congress with bipartisan backing and is now the 64th US national park. item.title: Marine life in Gulf of Mexico has still not fully recovered from 2010 BP oil spill
item.description: New study reveals dramatic population drops in fish, cephalopods and more after the Deepwater Horizon spill Marine life in the Gulf of Mexico plummeted by about 60% after BP’s 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill and has still not fully recovered, according to a new study . The April 2010 explosion of an offshore drilling unit 50 miles off the Louisiana coast triggered the largest marine oil spill in history, releasing 134m gallons of oil into the ocean. item.description: Scientists discovered a rock in Papua New Guinea that plunged more than 90 kilometers beneath Earth's surface, revealing a bizarre temperature pattern that challenges established theories of Earth's interior. item.title: AI listens to bee buzzes to monitor activity without lethal traps
item.description: Populations of many pollinators, including bumblebees, have been crashing over the last few decades, thanks to the widespread use of chemical pesticides, loss of habitat and the acceleration of climate change. But it can be hard to know just how bad the problem is, or whether conservation strategies are helping, without relying on lethal traps—which can kill tens of thousands of bees in order to get an accurate count of their populations. item.title: Reexamined Viking 2 signal reveals possible marsquake from region active decades later
item.description: Earthquakes and the seismic waves they generate provide some of the best clues to Earth's interior. To extend that success to other worlds, scientists placed seismometers on the Apollo missions to the moon and on the Viking Mars landers, which reached Mars in 1976. Though the Apollo detectors proved a resounding success, Viking's results on Mars were less clear: Viking 1's seismometer failed to deploy properly, and Viking 2 recorded only two ambiguous events. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How life on Earth experiences climate change
item.description: Climate change can look very different at the scale of a forest, field or hillside. A new review shows how changes in vegetation and atmospheric conditions can cause local microclimates to warm at very different rates from the regional climate—and why this matters for understanding how biodiversity will respond to climate change. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: World set to breach 1.5°C warming limit set by Paris Climate Agreement
item.description: The UN is warning that global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals of 1.5 degrees Celsius warming – and put the world on course for 2.6C warming this century. The report by the United Nations Environment Programme lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November's COP31 climate summit - set to take place next month in Turkey. Story by Emerald Maxwell. Fuente: France 24 - English.

item.title: Es necesario recortar las emisiones un 18 % en cuatro años para limitar el pico de temperatura a 1,7 grados
item.description: El mundo superará el umbral de 1,5 °C fijado en el Acuerdo de París, pero el pico de calentamiento podría limitarse a 1,7-1,8 °C si las emisiones caen un 18 % para 2030, un 45 % para 2035 y un 69 % cinco años después. Las emisiones globales se estancaron en 2025, pero las de Estados Unidos crecieron 133 megatoneladas, el mayor aumento de cualquier país, y su retirada del Acuerdo de París es una de las causas de que las proyecciones empeoren respecto al año pasado. Fuente: Noticias ONU.

item.title: Ancient wildfire study offers warning for a warming world
item.description: New research from the University of Aberdeen has revealed that periods of global warming can trigger long-lasting increases in wildfire activity, with ecosystems taking far longer to recover than previously thought. The study, recently published in Scientific Reports, provides the first detailed evidence of how wildfires responded to a major natural warming event around 65 million years ago, the Danian hyperthermal. This work offers important insights into the risks facing today's world as climate change drives more frequent and severe fires. Fuente: Phys.org.
